senses.subdomain: Regions Below the Surface of the Earth
senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of ἄβυσσος ‘pit,’ not occurring in the NT) a location of the dead and a place where the Devil is kept (Revelation 20:3), the abode of the beast as the antichrist (Revelation 11:7), and of Abaddon, as the angel of the underworld (Revelation 9:11)
senses.comment: ἄβυσσος is sometimes rendered as ‘a very deep hole’; in other instances, ‘a hole without a bottom’ or ‘the deepest hole in the earth.’

senses.def: ancestor of the human race

senses.subdomain: To Choose, To Select, To Prefer
senses.def: to choose or select for the purpose of showing special favor to or concern for
to refuse to recognize the force or power of something
senses.comment: In both Matthew 15:6 and Mark 7:13 the emphasis is upon the fact that people had regarded traditions as having greater authority than the word of God.

senses.def: to cut down grass or grain in a field
senses.comment: In biblical times mowing would have been done by means of a scythe or sickle, instruments with curved blades especially appropriate for cutting grass or standing grain.

senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of ἀναθάλλω ‘to bloom again,’ not occurring in the NT) to be in a state identical with a previous state
glosses: to be again in a position to
to be as one was formerly

senses.def: to explain something, presumably by putting forward additional or different information

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: (derivative of ἀνομία ‘to live lawlessly,’ 88.139) pertaining to living without regard to law, in the sense of refusing to obey laws
pertaining to being without the Law (specifically the first five books of the OT)
senses.comment: Even from the two contexts of 1 Corinthians 9:21 and Romans 2:12, it should be clear that ἄνομος[b] and ἀνόμως carry quite different implications in different contexts. In 1 Corinthians 9:21 a phrase such as ‘without the Law’ must be understood in the sense of ‘not being under obligation to the Law’ or ‘not being bound by the Law,’ and so 1 Corinthians 9:21 must be translated in a number of languages as ‘with those who are not bound by the Law, I live as one who is not bound by the Law,’ referring in these instances to the Law of Moses. It is important, however, in rendering the expression ‘not bound by the Law’ to avoid a phrase which would mean ‘lawless’ or ‘heedless of the Law.’ In the case of Romans 2:12, the phrase ‘without the Law’ must refer to those who are ignorant of the Law and thus are not bound by it, and so Romans 2:12 must be rendered in some languages as ‘those who sin without knowing anything about the Law are lost, but quite apart from any relationship to the Law.’|For another interpretation of ἄνομος in 1 Corinthians 9:21, see 11.42.

senses.domain: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes
senses.def: a non-Jew who lives completely without reference to the Jewish Law
senses.comment: For another interpretation of ἄνομος in 1 Corinthians 9:21, see 33.57.|In a number of contexts, it may be best to speak of ‘Gentiles’ as ‘those who are not Jews.’ In some languages the equivalent of ‘Gentiles’ is simply ‘foreigners,’ but one must be very certain that the use of a term meaning ‘foreigners’ will actually designate non-Jews rather than those people who do not speak the particular receptor language.|It would be a serious mistake to render ἄνομος as ‘lawless’ on the basis of its etymology. To speak of a ‘lawless person’ is to imply that he transgresses existing laws rather than being one who is not subject to the Mosaic Law.

senses.def: to lose the capacity to feel shame or embarrassment
glosses: to lose a feeling of shame

senses.def: to cause or instigate divisions between people
senses.comment: ‘To cause divisions’ may be expressed in a number of languages in idiomatic ways, for example, ‘to cause people to turn their backs on one another’ or ‘to cause people to no longer speak to one another’ or ‘to cause people to form parties against one another.’ For another interpretation of ἀποδιορίζω in Jude 1:19, see 30.116.

senses.subdomain: To Distinguish, To Evaluate, To Judge
senses.def: to judge that there is a significant distinction between two or more objects or events
senses.comment: In Jude 1:19 the specific distinction between ‘spiritual and unspiritual persons’ comes from the context, as suggested in the New English Bible. For another interpretation of ἀποδιορίζω in Jude 1:19, see 39.16.

senses.def: to bring an activity to a successful finish
senses.comment: It is also possible to translate ἀποτελέω in Luke 13:32 as ‘am performing,’ but the focus evidently is upon the completion of a series of such healings. The final phrase of Luke 13:32, καὶ τῇ τρίτω τελειοῦμαι ‘and on the third day I will be finished,’ points to a possible distinction between ἀποτελέω and τελειόω, in which the first apparently serves to mark the end of a particular series, while the second points to the completion of anything and everything involved.

senses.def: to say that one does not know about or is in any way related to a person or event
senses.comment: In translating ἀρνέομαι[a] and ἀπαρνέομαι[a], one can often use an equivalent phrase such as ‘to say that one does not know’ or ‘to say that one has nothing to do with.’|In denying an event, as in Luke 8:45, it may be possible to translate ‘but they all said they knew nothing about it.’ It is also possible to deny having done something, and therefore one may translate the response in Luke 8:45 as ‘but they all said that they did not do it’ or ‘… that they did not touch him.’

senses.def: to deny any relationship of association with someone
senses.comment: In a number of languages one may best translate ‘deny’ as ‘to make manifest not to know.’ Accordingly, one may translate the first part of Luke 12:9 as ‘whoever shows people that he does not know me’ or ‘whoever refuses to admit that he does know me.’ Denial need not involve some verbal formulation, though in some languages this is the most common practice. See also 33.277.

senses.def: to refuse to agree or consent to something

senses.subdomain: To Think About, with the Implied Purpose of Responding Appropriately
senses.def: to refuse to give thought to or express concern for
senses.comment: There are a number of problems involved in rendering appropriately ἀρνέομαι[d] and ἀπαρνέομαι[b] as in Luke 9:23 and Mark 8:34.|In a number of languages it simply makes no sense to translate ‘to say No to oneself,’ nor is it possible in many instances to use an expression such as ‘to deny oneself,’ since it almost always implies to deny oneself something. Sometimes the meaning may be expressed in a figurative or idiomatic manner, for example, ‘to refuse to pay attention to what one’s own desires are saying’ or ‘to refuse to think about what one just wants for oneself.’ In certain instances other kinds of idioms may be employed, for example, ‘to put oneself at the end of the line’ or even ‘to say to one’s heart, Keep quiet.’

senses.def: to refuse to follow someone as a leader

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: to behave in a way which is untrue to one’s real self, in a sense of denying certain valid aspects of one’s personality
senses.comment: It is possible in some languages to translate ‘he cannot be false to himself’ in 2 Timothy 2:13 as ‘he cannot be different from what he really is’ or ‘he cannot be otherwise than good.’

senses.def: pertaining to having no spot or stain

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of ἄσπιλος[a] ‘spotless, without stain,’ 79.59) pertaining to being without that which might mar one’s moral character
pertaining to the very act of doing something
to wash (in some contexts, possibly by dipping into water), with a view to making objects ritually acceptable
senses.comment: There is some doubt as to the precise extent to which βαπτίζω, καταβαπτίζω, and βαπτισμός in Mark 7:4 involve ritual cleansing, but the context would seem to imply this, particularly in view of the relationship of such washing to the rules followed by Jews in general and Pharisees in particular.

senses.def: to employ water in a religious ceremony designed to symbolize purification and initiation on the basis of repentance
senses.comment: According to the Didache (early second century) different forms of baptism were practiced in the early church, but with evident preference given to immersion.|The baptism practiced by John the Baptist would seem to reflect far more the Jewish pattern of ritual washing than the type of baptism employed by Christians, which constituted a symbol of initiation into the Christian community on the basis of belief in and loyalty to Jesus Christ as Lord and Savior. There seems, however, to be no reason to employ a different expression for baptism in the case of John than in the case of the early Christians. Most translators actually employ a transliterated form of the Greek term βαπτίζω, but in some languages this is both awkward as well as inappropriate, especially if another term or expression has already been employed and is widely accepted by groups practicing various types or forms of baptism. In some languages, for example, one may employ an expression such as ‘to enter the water’ or ‘to undergo the ritual involving water.’ Such expressions do not necessarily imply the quantity of water nor the particular means by which water is applied.

senses.def: a village near Jerusalem, perhaps east of Bethany
(an idiom, literally: to throw a bridle on) to place restrictions upon someone’s behavior
senses.comment: It may, however, be important in some languages to express more clearly the intent involved, and therefore one might wish to translate this clause in 1 Corinthians 7:35 as ‘my purpose is not to try to control you’ or ‘… to tell you just what you must do.’

senses.def: to bring under control and to continue to restrain
senses.comment: In many languages it may be difficult to speak of ‘bringing a person under control.’ It may therefore be more appropriate to use some such phrase as ‘not allow a person to do just what he wants’ or ‘make a person behave’ or ‘make a person obey.’ In speaking of animals, one may render James 3:7 as ‘all kinds of wild animals … can be made to obey a person.’

senses.def: to make something known by making evident what was either unknown before or what may have been difficult to understand
to make something evident or clear by explanation
glosses: to make clear to make evident

senses.def: to sail through an area from one side to the other
to state something with firmness and certainty
a female slave
to express an unusually high degree of confidence in someone or something being exceptionally noteworthy
senses.comment: Whether in any particular context the boasting is legitimate or not depends upon what is boasted about. In a number of languages, however, quite different terms are employed, depending upon the differing degrees of justification for such boasting.

senses.def: to carry out a custom or tradition
glosses: to be in the habit of

senses.def: a degree which is considerably in excess of some point on an implied or explicit scale of extent
the son of Abiud in the genealogy of Jesus
the son of Melea in the genealogy of Jesus
to provide instruction and training, with the implication of skill in some area of practical knowledge
pertaining to having awakened
senses.comment: In some languages the process of waking up is described idiomatically as ‘when his mind came back to him’ or ‘when his eyes opened.’

senses.subdomain: Cloth, Leather, and Objects Made of Such Materials
senses.def: a piece of cloth sewed on clothing to repair a hole or tear
senses.comment: The statement in Matthew 9:16 that ‘no one puts a patch of new cloth on an old garment’ seems almost preposterous or incredible in some societies, since people habitually repair old clothing by putting on patches of new cloth, sometimes to the point where it is difficult to determine what was the original fabric. In Matthew 9:16 the phrase ῥάκους ἀγνάφου, often translated ‘new cloth,’ is literally ‘unshrunken cloth,’ in other words, cloth which has not been washed one or more times and thus has been shrunken in the process. In biblical times there was no technique for preshrinking cloth.

senses.def: any kind of food or nourishment
senses.comment: Almost all languages have at least a few general terms for food, though these may be derived from verbal expressions meaning essentially ‘that which is eaten.’ In some instances a distinction may be made between ‘that which is chewed’ and ‘that which is drunk,’ and it may therefore be important in certain contexts to speak of food in general by a phrase meaning ‘that which is either chewed or drunk.’ If one fails to include both types of food, the reader might interpret a passage such as Matthew 6:11 as requesting only solid foods.|In the place of a general term or phrase such as ‘that which is eaten’ or ‘that which is consumed,’ some languages generalize the meaning of a particular term. For example, in certain parts of the Orient the term meaning specifically ‘rice’ also refers to ‘food’ in general. In fact, some persons will declare, ‘I have not eaten!’ if they have not had rice as part of a meal. A similar type of meaning has developed in English with respect to ‘bread.’ For example, in rendering Luke 4:4 (οὐκ ἐπ’ ἄρτῳ μόνῳ ζήσεται ὁ ἄνθρωπος ‘man shall not live by bread alone’) it would be wrong to employ a strictly literal rendering, since this might mean simply that people should not live on a diet consisting solely of bread. The meaning of Luke 4:4 is, of course, ‘to live means more than merely eating.’

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: to cause someone to feel resentment

senses.subdomain: Agent in a Causative Role Marked by Verbs
senses.def: a marker of a causative relation, with the implication of stimulating a change in motivation or attitude
senses.comment: The relevant action in 2 Corinthians 9:2b comes from the immediately preceding statements in 2 Corinthians 9:1-2 Corinthians 9:2a.

senses.def: to follow a straight course to one’s destination or goal
a pleasant or sweet-smelling odor
senses.comment: Since the reference in Philippians 4:18 is to a sacrifice, the use of εὐωδία may seem strange, if not contradictory, in many languages, since the odor from burning flesh is normally not regarded as being fragrant or pleasant. It may therefore be necessary to include a marginal note to explain this usage.

senses.def: a Hebrew term meaning my God
senses.comment: For certain problems involved in rendering an expression such as ‘my God,’ see the discussion in 12.1.

senses.def: that on which a structure is built
senses.comment: In some languages it is possible to describe a typical foundation in ancient times as ‘large stones underneath the walls.’ In other languages, however, this may seem to be quite a meaningless type of expression, since foundations are only made secure by driving stakes deep into the ground. Therefore, it may be best to describe the function of a foundation by ‘what keeps the walls firm’ or ‘how the walls are made not to move’ or ‘what goes beneath the walls.’

senses.def: a stone used in the construction of a foundation
senses.comment: Such foundation stones may be described as ‘stones beneath the walls’ or ‘stones beneath the walls to make the walls strong.’

senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of θεμέλιος[a] ‘foundation,’ 7.41) the basis for some action or event

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: (derivative of θυμός[a] ‘anger,’ 88.178) to be extremely angry, even to the point of being in a rage
senses.comment: In some instances it may be possible to speak of ‘being extremely angry’ as ‘to be so angry as not to be able to think.’

senses.subdomain: Cloth, Leather, and Objects Made of Such Materials
senses.def: any kind of clothing
a king of Judah mentioned in the genealogy of Jesus
one who teaches what is good and morally right

senses.domain: Stances and Events Related to Stances
senses.def: to cause someone to assume a reclining (or possibly sitting) position as part of the process of eating
glosses: to cause to recline to eat
to have someone sit down to eat

senses.domain: Stances and Events Related to Stances
senses.def: to be in a reclining position as one eats (with the focus either upon the position or the act of eating)
to experience strong physical desires, particularly of a sexual nature
(derivative of κελεύω ‘to command,’ 33.323) the voicing of a command
senses.comment: In a number of languages the expression ‘at the word of command’ may be rendered as ‘when the command is given’ or ‘when the command is shouted.’

senses.def: a more or less tender, flexible branch, as of a vine
(a diminutive derivative of κόρη ‘girl,’ not occurring in the NT, but seemingly having lost the diminutive feature of meaning) a girl about the age of puberty
senses.comment: In Mark 5:41 κοράσιον is equated in meaning with the Aramaic term ταλιθα (see 9.48), and in Mark 5:42 this girl is identified as being twelve years of age. Compare also ἠνέχθη ἡ κεφαλὴ αὐτοῦ ἐπὶ πίνακι καὶ ἐδόθη τῷ κορασίῳ ‘his head was brought in on a plate and given to the girl’ (Matthew 14:11). It is impossible to determine the age of Herodias’ daughter, but in view of her role as an attractive dancer, she was probably of the age of puberty.

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: trickery that results from craftiness (κυβεία literally refers to dice playing)
a teacher and prophet at Antioch
a person sending greetings in Romans 16:21
a degree which surpasses in some manner a point on an explicit or implicit scale of extent
a marker of contrast indicating an alternative
the father of Λευί[c] in the genealogy of Jesus
the father of Neri in the genealogy of Jesus
the father of Aminadam in the genealogy of Jesus (Luke 3:33, apparatus)

senses.domain: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products
senses.def: the front part of the head above the eyes
senses.comment: Though in most languages there is a specific term to designate the forehead, it may be necessary in some instances to speak of ‘the upper face’ or ‘the face above the eyes.’

senses.def: to cause something to become dirty or soiled
to cause something to be ceremonially impure, with the implication of serious defilement
the process of dying
senses.comment: In a number of languages clear distinctions are made in the use of terms for dying on the basis of the manner or circumstances of death. For example, one term may refer to death primarily as the result of old age, while another term may refer to death caused by sickness, and still other terms may be used for death caused by violence. Careful distinctions must be used in determining the choice of terms based on particular contexts.|This first clause of 2 Corinthians 4:10 is highly elliptical, for it evidently refers to the fact that Paul was constantly in danger of dying in the same manner in which Jesus died, that is to say, by violence. One may render 2 Corinthians 4:10 as ‘at all times we live in the constant threat of being killed as Jesus was.’

senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of νέκρωσις[a] ‘death,’ 23.99) the state of not being able to bear children as the result of having passed through menopause
a woman who is about to be married or who has just been married
senses.comment: As in the case of ‘bridegroom’ (10.56), it may be necessary in some languages to indicate with ‘bride’ whether the person has just been married or is about to be married.

senses.def: the wife of one’s son
senses.comment: For languages which do not have specific terms for ‘mother- in-law’ and ‘daughter-in-law’ it may be possible to render Luke 12:53 by translating ‘women will be against the wives of their sons, and young women will be against the mothers of their husbands.’

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: (derivative of οἰκτίρω ‘to have mercy,’ 88.80) pertaining to showing mercy or compassion
senses.comment: In a number of languages expressions involving showing mercy or being merciful are expressed in highly idiomatic ways, for example, ‘to show one’s heart toward,’ ‘to feel in one’s stomach for,’ ‘to have one’s heart go out toward,’ or ‘to treat as a loving child.’

senses.def: pertaining to actual existence
a marker of discourse content, whether direct or indirect
senses.comment: The marking of direct and indirect discourse varies greatly from language to language. In some instances there is no marker at all; in other cases one marker precedes and another follows. In still other instances a repetition of an expression of speaking occurs at the end of a quotation, whether direct or indirect. In a number of languages written usage differs appreciably from spoken usage, because intonation so often marks introduced discourse in the spoken form of a language.

senses.def: a marker of cause or reason, based on an evident fact
glosses: in view of the fact that

senses.subdomain: Markers of Identificational and Explanatory Clauses [Epexegetical]
senses.def: a marker of identificational and explanatory clauses

senses.subdomain: Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young
senses.def: the state of being old, with the implication of obsolescence
senses.comment: For a somewhat different interpretation of παλαιότης in Romans 7:6, see 58.74.

senses.def: the state of that which is old, obsolete, and hence inferior and unsatisfactory (in contrast with that which is either καινός[b] or νέος[b] ‘new,’ 58.71)
to cause someone to become consoled

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: a state of being quite angry and upset at something
to move about from place to place, with significant changes in direction
senses.comment: In order to communicate the meaning of ‘to wander about’ or ‘to travel about,’ it may be necessary to be rather specific, for example, ‘they first go in one direction and then in another’ or ‘they first go to one place and then off to another.’

senses.def: to take along or to bring along on a journey or as one travels about
glosses: to bring along on a trip

senses.def: an evergreen aromatic plant used for seasoning
senses.comment: In the parallel passage (Matthew 23:23) ἄνηθον ‘dill’ and κύμινον ‘cumin’ occur (see 3.24-3.25).|In designating ‘rue’ as well as ἡδύοσμον 'mint', ἄνηθον ‘dill,’ and κύμινον ‘cumin,’ it is probably wise to borrow a term and use a classifier, for example, ‘a seasoning herb called rue.’

senses.def: to strike or hit an object, one or more times
senses.comment: In Revelation 8:12 the emphasis seems to be upon the damage caused to the sun rather than the actual fact of a blow, but the use of πλήσσω seems to indicate that the damage is the result of some type of blow.

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: one who engages in sexual immorality, whether a man or a woman, and in some contexts, distinguished from an adulterer or adulteress
to give in advance of some other event
senses.comment: It is possible to render Romans 11:35 as ‘who has ever given God something before God gave something?’

senses.def: to earn or to gain something in addition
senses.comment: As in the case of Luke 19:18 (see 57.189), it may be necessary to change the form of expression so as to introduce a personal agent, for example, ‘I have earned ten minas with the one you gave me.’ In some languages it may be necessary to say ‘I did business with the one mina and now I have ten’ or ‘… it has become ten minas.’

senses.def: pertaining to divinely inspired utterances
(a borrowing from Aramaic) a Jewish teacher and scholar recognized for expertise in interpreting the Jewish Scriptures

senses.subdomain: Cloth, Leather, and Objects Made of Such Materials
senses.def: a heavy material normally used for making sacks, but worn by persons in mourning and as a sign of repentance
senses.comment: In most languages sackcloth is described as ‘coarse cloth’ and sometimes as ‘heavy cloth.’

senses.def: to cause something to be both specific and clear
pertaining to being in a state of darkness
senses.comment: In some languages ‘dark’ may be most satisfactorily expressed as ‘without light.’

senses.def: the dense spiky cluster in which the seeds of grain such as wheat and barley grow (restricted in NT contexts to references to wheat)
senses.comment: In some languages it is impossible to speak of ‘a head of wheat’ or ‘an ear of wheat,’ since terms referring to ‘head’ and ‘ear’ have no such figurative extensions of meaning. In certain instances the equivalent may be ‘the point of the wheat’ or ‘the brush of the wheat,’ referring to the spike-like objects which extend from each grain.

senses.subdomain: Not Able To Be Known, Secret
senses.def: to cause something to remain unknown by means of purposeful concealment
to fall together in a heap
to decide with someone else that something is preferable or good

senses.subdomain: Instruments Used in Marking and Writing
senses.def: to use a seal to close or to make something secure
senses.comment: For a discussion of some of the translational problems involved with ‘seal,’ see 6.54.

senses.def: (derivative of σφραγίς[c] ‘mark, seal,’ 33.483) to put a mark on something, primarily to indicate ownership but possibly also to mark group identity
to arrange to give something to someone in a secure manner
glosses: to turn over to in a secure way
to give in a secure manner
senses.comment: For a somewhat different interpretation of σφραγίζω in Romans 15:28, see 15.189.

senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of σφραγίζω[a] ‘to seal,’ 6.55) to deliver something safely to a destination
senses.comment: It is also possible that σφραγισάμενος in Romans 15:28 serves to confirm the significance of the collection which has been raised. For a somewhat different interpretation of σφραγίζω in Romans 15:28, see 57.87.

senses.def: (derivative of σφραγίς[e] ‘validation,’ 73.9) to demonstrate by authentic proof the truth or validity of something
to give birth to a child
senses.comment: All languages have expressions for human birth, though these are frequently in idiomatic forms, for example, ‘to drop a child’ or ‘to cause a baby to pass between the legs.’ A number of languages have a variety of terms referring to giving birth, and some of these may involve unfortunate connotations. One must therefore be careful about the selection of appropriate expressions.

senses.def: an emphatic marker of result, often associated with exhortation
to punish by physical torture or torment
an extraordinary degree, involving a considerable excess over what would be expected (this series differs from the series in 78.31 primarily in emphasizing the excessive degree)
senses.comment: In order that something of the irony of the phrase τῶν ὑπερλίαν ἀποστόλων (2 Corinthians 11:5) may be indicated, one may wish to follow the example of Today’s English Version and translate “I do not think that I am the least bit inferior to those very special so-called ‘apostles’ of yours!”

senses.def: pertaining to being final in a series, but probably not as emphatic as ἔσχατος[a] ‘last,’ 61.13

senses.subdomain: A Point of Time with Reference to Other Points of Time: Before, Long Ago, Now, At the Same Time, When, About, After
senses.def: pertaining to a subsequent event, but not necessarily the second in a series
to kiss, either as an expression of greeting or as a sign of special affection and appreciation
to move quickly from a point or area in order to avoid presumed danger or difficulty

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: (comparative of κακός[a] ‘bad,’ 88.106) pertaining to being worse in the sense of being harmful and damaging
pertaining to being less satisfactory than something else
a song of praise (in the NT probably a reference to an OT psalm)
